# Who is Mistaken?
###### Abstract
Recognizing when people have false beliefs is crucial for understanding their actions. We introduce the novel problem of identifying when people in abstract scenes have incorrect beliefs. We present a dataset of scenes, each visually depicting an 8-frame story in which a character has a mistaken belief. We then create a representation of characters’ beliefs for two tasks in human action understanding: predicting who is mistaken, and when they are mistaken. Experiments suggest that our method for identifying mistaken characters performs better on these tasks than simple baselines.
## 3 Dataset
We collected a dataset of abstract scenes to study beliefs of characters. Each scene in our dataset consists of a sequence of 8 frames showing an everyday situation. One or more people believe something incorrectly about their environment in each scene. A person may have a false belief for many reasons, including occlusion and misinterpreting intentions. Although the characters inside the scenes do not know if they are mistaken, we designed the dataset so that third-party viewers can clearly recognize who is mistaken.

# Seeing vs. Believing: Evaluating the Language Bias of Open-Source MLLMs in Counter-Intuitive Scenes
###### Abstract
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in mainstream visual understanding tasks, but their ability to process action scenes that contradict everyday common sense remains undertested. To address this gap, we introduce CAIT, a benchmark comprising 400 high-fidelity synthetic scenes focused on counter-intuitive visual actions, such as “a rabbit is chasing a tiger”, where visual evidence explicitly contradicts common-sense expectations.
Further analysis demonstrates that this failure is driven by a strong language prior: rather than trusting the visual input, they automatically override the anomalous visual signals with statistically common text descriptions. context.title: UC San Diego researchers teach a 7B AI agent to read its partner's mind
context.snippet:
UC San Diego researchers give a 7B AI agent theory of mind, boosting Sotopia scores by about 11.5% and BigToM belief accuracy by 26.7 points.
Testing covered language-only benchmarks, Sotopia and BigToM, plus the multimodal MMRole benchmark, which brings in more than just text. On Sotopia, which evaluates social interaction skills, the Qwen2.5-7B agent posted an average relative gain of approximately 11.5% across partner settings. That figure measures improvement relative to a baseline, not an absolute score. The bigger jump came on BigToM, a test of belief tracking. There, the approach delivered an average gain of 26.7 percentage points on paired true-belief and false-belief accuracy. The authors have released their code publicly, so other researchers can probe the results directly rather than taking the paper’s word for it. Why smaller agents matter here This paper tries to give a modest 7B model a specific social skill through better training structure, not sheer scale. Smaller models are cheaper to run and easier to deploy on limited hardware. Many approaches to reasoning about other agents rely on auxiliary systems running alongside the main model at inference time. Baking the capability into the policy itself sidesteps that overhead. What this means The most obvious stakeholders are developers building multi-agent systems. An agent that can estimate what its counterpart believes, including mistaken beliefs, is better positioned to coordinate and can correct misunderstandings. Those are exactly the social interaction skills Sotopia is designed to measure. The MMRole results suggest the approach is meant to extend beyond pure text, though the strongest headline numbers in the research come from the language benchmarks. A relative improvement of approximately 11.5% on Sotopia is meaningful, but it is a step forward on a specific test, not a solved problem.

# Who is Mistaken?

Carl Vondrick Antonio Torralba Benjamin Eysenbach
...
### Abstract
Recognizing when people have false beliefs is crucial for understanding their actions. We introduce the novel problem of identifying when people in abstract scenes have incorrect beliefs. We present a dataset of scenes, each visually depicting an 8-frame story in which a character has a mistaken belief. We then create a representation of characters' beliefs for two tasks in human action understanding: predicting who is mistaken, and when they are mistaken. Experiments suggest that our method for identifying mistaken characters performs better on these tasks than simple baselines. Diagnostics on our model suggest it learns important cues for recognizing mistaken beliefs, such as gaze. We believe models of people's beliefs will have many applications in action understanding, robotics, and healthcare.

exa.snippet:
###### Abstract

Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider–Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is reality bias, which accounts for 60% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4409058/)Abstract

The capability of adult and child witnesses to accurately recollect events from the past and provide reliable testimony has been hotly debated for more than 100 years. Prominent legal cases of the 1980s and 1990s sparked lengthy debates and important research questions surrounding the fallibility and general reliability of memory. But what lessons have we learned, some 35 years later, about the role of memory in the judicial system? In this review, we focus on what we now know about the consequences of the fallibility of memory for legal proceedings. We present a brief historical overview of false memories that focuses on three critical forensic areas that changed memory research: children as eyewitnesses, historic sexual abuse and eyewitness (mis)identification. We revisit some of the prominent trials of the 1980s and 1990s to not only consider the role false memories have played in judicial decisions, but also to see how this has helped us understand memory today. Finally, we consider the way in which the research on memory (true and false) has been successfully integrated into some courtroom procedures.

keenable.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind

keenable.title: Seeing vs. Believing: Evaluating the Language Bias of Open-Source MLLMs in Counter-Intuitive Scenes
keenable.snippet: We propose UAIT (Uncommon-sense Action Image-Text) dataset, a new evaluation benchmark designed to test the semantic understanding ability of visual language models (VLMs) in uncommon-sense action scenes. Unlike previous datasets that focus on common visual scenes with statistical frequency advantages, UAIT challenges models with grammatically reasonable but semantically counter-common sense image-text pairs. Such tasks require models to go beyond superficial pattern recognition and demonstrate a deep understanding of agent-patient relationships and physical feasibility. keenable.title: Brain-Aligned Multimodal LLMs for Social and Emotional Understanding of Cartoon Movies
keenable.snippet: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions.

keenable.title: Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? Humor "Understanding" Benchmarks from The New Yorker Caption Contest
keenable.snippet: Large neural networks can now generate jokes, but do they really "understand" humor? We challenge AI models with three tasks derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest: matching a joke to a cartoon, identifying a winning caption, and explaining why a winning caption is funny. These tasks encapsulate progressively more sophisticated aspects of "understanding" a cartoon; key elements are the complex, often surprising relationships between images and captions and the frequent inclusion of indirect and playful allusions to human experience and culture. We investigate both multimodal and language-only models: the former are challenged with the cartoon images directly, while the latter are given multifaceted descriptions of the visual scene to simulate human-level visual understanding. We find that both types of models struggle at all three tasks. For example, our best multimodal models fall 30 accuracy points behind human performance on the matching task, and, even when provided ground-truth visual scene descriptors, human-authored explanations are preferred head-to-head over the best machine-authored ones (few-shot GPT-4) in more than 2/3 of cases. We release models, code, leaderboard, and corpus, which includes newly-gathered annotations describing the image's locations/entities, what's unusual in the scene, and an explanation of the joke.

keenable.title: Who is Mistaken?
keenable.snippet: Recognizing when people have false beliefs is crucial for understanding their actions. We introduce the novel problem of identifying when people in abstract scenes have incorrect beliefs. We present a dataset of scenes, each visually depicting an 8-frame story in which a character has a mistaken belief. We then create a representation of characters' beliefs for two tasks in human action understanding: predicting who is mistaken, and when they are mistaken. Experiments suggest that our method for identifying mistaken characters performs better on these tasks than simple baselines. Diagnostics on our model suggest it learns important cues for recognizing mistaken beliefs, such as gaze. We believe models of people's beliefs will have many applications in action understanding, robotics, and healthcare.

keenable.title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
keenable.snippet: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs’ performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

Title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind

Authors: Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Syed Talal Wasim, Juergen Gall, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.

Title: It's Not What the Image Shows: Irrelevant Context Destabilises VLM Judges Without Informing Them

Authors: Nagham Omar, Mahmoud Jabarin, Kinan Ibraheem, Lotem Peled-Cohen

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in place of human annotators, making it important that substitutability tests reflect the model rather than incidental evaluation conditions. We introduce MIST, the Misleading-Image Stress Test: 200 English sentences, each built around a phrase readable either figuratively or literally and shown with an aligned image depicting its reading, a misleading image depicting the opposite, or no image at all. The guidelines require the label to be decided from the sentence alone, so no image should change any answer. We expected each image to pull a judge's labels toward the sense it depicts, and neither kind did. Across thirteen VLM judges, an aligned image changed 20.5% of labels and a misleading one 19.4%, close for every judge and both above the 11.6% produced by deleting the ignore-the-image instruction with the image left in place. Yet only 37% of the labels that differ between the two images moved toward the sense shown, and agreement with our human annotators is unchanged whether the image is absent, aligned or misleading. The effect is smaller in the seven judges that pass the alt-test than in the six that never do, but present in all of them: what moves a judge is that an image is there, not which of the two it is, so a substitutability verdict describes a configuration as much as a model.

Abstract: Large Vision Language Models have integrated reasoning capabilities, elevating cognitive performance to new levels. However, existing evaluations either focus solely on perception or rely on specific domains such as maths or coding. Evaluation for reasoning capabilities that align with an open-world environment is still required, especially one that considers perception and reasoning jointly. Authors: Qi Song, Honglin Li, Yingchen Yu, Haoyi Zhou, Lin Yang, Song Bai, Qi She, Zilong Huang, Yunqing Zhao

Abstract: Recent releases such as o3 highlight human-like "thinking with images" reasoning that combines tool use with stepwise verification, yet most open-source approaches still rely on text-only chains, rigid visual schemas, or single-step pipelines, limiting flexibility, interpretability, and transferability on complex tasks. We introduce CodeDance, which explores executable code as a general solver for visual reasoning. Unlike fixed-schema calls (e.g., only predicting bounding-box coordinates), CodeDance defines, composes, and executes code to orchestrate multiple tools, compute intermediate results, and render visual artifacts (e.g., boxes, lines, plots) that support transparent, self-checkable reasoning. Interestingly, beyond the expected capabilities taught by atomic supervision, we empirically observe novel emergent behaviors during RL training: CodeDance demonstrates novel tool invocations, unseen compositions, and cross-task transfer. These behaviors arise without task-specific fine-tuning, suggesting a general and scalable mechanism for executable visual reasoning. Extensive experiments across reasoning benchmarks (e.g., visual search, math, chart QA) show that CodeDance not only consistently outperforms schema-driven and text-only baselines, but also surpasses closed models such as GPT-4o and larger open-source models.

parallel-fast.snippet:
Abstract

Vision–language models (VLMs) have made remarkable progress in visual reasoning during the last decade. Most evaluations have used simple scenes (MS-COCO) that do not showcase complex human interactions or behaviors, only a handful of non-curated human descriptions as a benchmark, and have not focused on understanding the model’s error types. Here, we introduce the Complex Social Behavior (CSB) dataset, containing 100 images depicting complex social interactions/behaviors. We analyze the progression of scene descriptions over a decade (2017-2025) of VLMs (four pre-Multimodal Large Language Models, MLLMs, and five MLLMs). We evaluate the accuracy of the models and 20 human descriptions relative to a gold standard on the CSB dataset and on a sample from MS-COCO. We analyzed five visual-cognitive error types: object detection, recognition, hallucination, scene understanding, and spatial dependence. The CSB dataset showed a more pronounced improvement than MS-COCO in scene description accuracy, with pre-MLLMs achieving much lower accuracy than the bottom-ranked human descriptions and MLLMs attaining accuracies similar to the top-ranked human descriptions. We show that MLLMs have eliminated the gap in scene description accuracy between simpler MS-COCO scenes and scenes depicting complex behaviors (CSB). MLLMs have almost eliminated all error types in our tested datasets, except for occasionally relying on different image regions for scene descriptions than humans do (spatial dependence error). We also show that detection, recognition, and hallucination errors have the highest impact on scene description accuracy. Together, our findings provide a more thorough evaluation of how visual language models have advanced over the last decade.

Abstract:Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually.

seltz.title: Vision models fail false-belief tests because they cannot see, not because they cannot reason
seltz.snippet:
## In one line

Visual theory of mind failures in vision-language models stem from a perceptual bottleneck, not a reasoning deficit.

Vision-language models, which process both images and text, often fail at a task called false belief: figuring out where someone thinks an object is, even if that belief is wrong. When the task is given as a story, these models do nearly as well as people. But when the same task is told through pictures, their performance drops sharply. Most researchers assumed the models lacked reasoning skills for beliefs.

This paper argues the real problem is perceptual: the models cannot reliably see what is happening in the images. The authors tested this by giving the models perfect written descriptions of the scenes. With those descriptions, the models did as well as or better than with text alone, proving they can reason correctly once they get the right visual information. The most common mistake was “reality bias,” reporting where an object actually is rather than where a missing agent believes it is, which accounted for 60% of failures.

This matters because it changes where to focus improvement. Instead of building better reasoning modules for beliefs, developers should improve how models extract structured information from visual scenes, such as tracking which characters are present at each moment. Fixing the perceptual pipeline could unlock human like social understanding in AI systems.

## Abstract

High text recognition performance does not guarantee that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) share human-like decision patterns when resolving ambiguity. We investigate this behavioral gap by directly comparing humans and VLMs using continuously interpolated Japanese character shapes generated via a ββ-VAE. We estimate decision boundaries in a single-character recognition (shape-only task) and evaluate whether VLM responses align with human judgments under shape in context (i.e., embedding an ambiguous character near the human decision boundary in word-level context). We find that human and VLM decision boundaries differ in the shape-only task, and that shape in context can improve human alignment in some conditions. seltz.snippet:
AI vision tools turn an image into input a language model can use, then generate a description or answer based on that visual input and the question. They can be useful for explaining a scene or reading a chart, but a fluent answer does not prove the system noticed the exact detail you asked about. Small text, rotated images, counts, positions and complex visual relationships are common points of failure. Treat the answer as an interpretation to check—not as a guarantee of what is in the picture.

## How does AI recognize what’s in a picture?

An image-capable AI system processes visual input into a representation that can be used alongside language. It then generates a text response conditioned on that input and the user’s question. This lets a person ask things such as “What is on the table?” or “Which line rises fastest?” without first converting the image into a written description.

That is a useful plain-language account, not a claim that every product works the same way. Services can differ in their image-processing components, how they handle resolution and detail, and how visual information is combined with language. The system is not necessarily inspecting an image as a person would; it produces an answer from the visual information available to it and the wording of the request.

For one concrete example, OpenAI’s image and vision API documentation describes image inputs and says its API may resize images and provides detail controls. Those implementation details apply to that API documentation, not to every image model. A tool’s answer can also be shaped by context in the prompt: if you suggest what an image contains, the response may reflect that suggestion as well as visual evidence.

Here's the problem with every \"Best Prompts\" list you've read: they were written by people who ran the prompt once, liked how it looked, and hit publish. Nobody tested 100. Nobody told you which ones failed or why.

ultimate.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
ultimate.snippet: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.

ultimate.title: Seeing vs. Believing: Evaluating the Language Bias of Open-Source MLLMs in Counter-Intuitive Scenes
ultimate.snippet: We propose UAIT (Uncommon-sense Action Image-Text) dataset, a new evaluation benchmark designed to test the semantic understanding ability of visual language models (VLMs) in uncommon-sense action scenes. Unlike previous datasets that focus on common visual scenes with statistical frequency advantages, UAIT challenges models with grammatically reasonable but semantically counter-common sense image-text pairs. Such tasks require models to go beyond superficial pattern recognition and demonstrate a deep understanding of agent-patient relationships and physical feasibility. To build UAIT, we designed a semi-automated process to synthesize high-quality uncommon-sense image-text samples using large language models, few-shot prompt engineering, and text-to-image generation. Each sample is accompanied by a carefully designed multiple-choice question to test the model's competence in fine-grained reasoning. We evaluate multiple state-of-the-art visual language models and compare them with models based on contrastive learning. Experiments show that all models perform significantly worse than humans in semantic judgment, especially in distinguishing grammatical correctness from semantic rationality. Further experiments show that even the lightweight model can improve its accuracy after fine-tuning, demonstrating the great potential of directional adaptation. This study not only reveals the key weaknesses of VLMs, but also provides diagnostic tools and research directions for the development of robust models with real visual semantic reasoning capabilities.

ultimate.title: Brain-Aligned Multimodal LLMs for Social and Emotional Understanding of Cartoon Movies
ultimate.snippet: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions.

ultimate.title: Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? Humor "Understanding" Benchmarks from The New Yorker Caption Contest
ultimate.snippet: Large neural networks can now generate jokes, but do they really "understand" humor? We challenge AI models with three tasks derived from the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest: matching a joke to a cartoon, identifying a winning caption, and explaining why a winning caption is funny. These tasks encapsulate progressively more sophisticated aspects of "understanding" a cartoon; key elements are the complex, often surprising relationships between images and captions and the frequent inclusion of indirect and playful allusions to human experience and culture. We investigate both multimodal and language-only models: the former are challenged with the cartoon images directly, while the latter are given multifaceted descriptions of the visual scene to simulate human-level visual understanding. We find that both types of models struggle at all three tasks. For example, our best multimodal models fall 30 accuracy points behind human performance on the matching task, and, even when provided ground-truth visual scene descriptors, human-authored explanations are preferred head-to-head over the best machine-authored ones (few-shot GPT-4) in more than 2/3 of cases. We release models, code, leaderboard, and corpus, which includes newly-gathered annotations describing the image's locations/entities, what's unusual in the scene, and an explanation of the joke.

Often, images in standard datasets are simple scenes (e.g., an image of a kitchen, desk, or beach scene) that do not include complex human actions or social interactions. Thus, the datasets may not capture the human behaviors and interactions that are critical to everyday visual inferences. Describing these complex scenes accurately might be more challenging for models than describing simple scenes from typical datasets.

To understand the shortcomings of these models, we developed a novel technique to classify model errors in image description generation. These errors included object detection errors, object recognition errors [39], hallucinations [37], scene understanding errors, and spatial dependence errors [10].

ultimate.title: Who is Mistaken?
ultimate.snippet: Recognizing when people have false beliefs is crucial for understanding their actions. We introduce the novel problem of identifying when people in abstract scenes have incorrect beliefs. We present a dataset of scenes, each visually depicting an 8-frame story in which a character has a mistaken belief. We then create a representation of characters' beliefs for two tasks in human action understanding: predicting who is mistaken, and when they are mistaken. Experiments suggest that our method for identifying mistaken characters performs better on these tasks than simple baselines. Diagnostics on our model suggest it learns important cues for recognizing mistaken beliefs, such as gaze. We believe models of people's beliefs will have many applications in action understanding, robotics, and healthcare.

ultimate.title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
ultimate.snippet: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs’ performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

webiq.title: [2611.10694] Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
webiq.snippet: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning.

This paper introduces a thoughtfully designed, two-stage diagnostic framework to evaluate the perception, rule-following, and internal simulation capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in grid-based board games (Chess, Gomoku, Xiangqi). We present a dataset of scenes, each visually depicting an 8-frame story in which a character has a mistaken belief. We then create a representation of characters' beliefs for two tasks in human action understanding: predicting who is mistaken, and when they are mistaken. Annotations were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk, resulting in over 1,200 high-quality sequences where characters have clear mistaken beliefs, verified by multiple human annotators. The study revealed several critical aspects of how models can learn Theory of Mind: Gaze as an Implicit Cue: The model learned to value gaze without explicit instruction. In ablation studies, flipping the character's pose (making them look away) caused performance to drop significantly, suggesting the model internally learned that "seeing is knowing."
Temporal Modeling: Because a "mistake" is often defined by past events (what a person saw or missed), the model employs a convolutional logistic regression across a sequence of frames. Using a temporal kernel of $K=7$, the model analyzes the "story" surrounding a moment to determine if a character's current belief is justified. Learning Tasks: The model was trained on two primary tasks: identifying who is mistaken and when the mistake occurs.
While this work establishes a foundation for recognizing mistaken beliefs, limitations remain. The model currently struggles with mistakes rooted in complex physics, such as an unbalanced see-saw. Future work aims to integrate explicit physical reasoning and transition from abstract scenes to natural, real-world videos using domain adaptation.
